toc.title: The Pod, its containers, init, sidecar and ephemeral containers

html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Explain what a Pod is and how its containers share resources
  • Describe init, sidecar and ephemeral containers and the three probes
  • Compare Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job and CronJob
  • Choose the right controller for a scenario

2The Pod, its containers, init, sidecar and ephemeral containers

Running case

Harbor Books Needs Its Shop Running

  • The platform engineer has the container images (module 1) and a cluster (module 2)
  • The shop has parts with different needs: a storefront and a catalog that can be replaced at will, a database that must keep its identity, a log collector for every node, and a nightly sales report
  • Today each part is a plain Pod: when one dies, nobody brings it back
  • In this module you will pick the right controller for each part

The Pod: the Smallest Deployable Unit

  • A Pod wraps one or more containers that share network and storage
  • The containers run together and are scheduled together on one node
  • They share one IP address and port space, so they reach each other on localhost
  • A Pod is ephemeral: it is never moved to another node, only replaced by a new Pod
  • You rarely create a Pod directly: a controller creates and replaces Pods for you

Exam tip

Kubernetes schedules and manages Pods, not single containers.

Init, Sidecar and Ephemeral Containers Moving

  • Init containers run one at a time, in order, and must finish before the app containers start
  • A sidecar container is an init container with restartPolicy: Always: it starts in the init sequence and keeps running beside the app
  • Ephemeral containers are added to a running Pod to debug it and are never restarted
  • As of 30 October 2026: native sidecar containers are stable since v1.33

Exam tip

Init containers finish and stop, sidecars keep running, and ephemeral containers exist only to debug.

3Pod phases, restart policy, probes

Pod Phases and Restart Policy

Phase What it means
Pending accepted by the cluster, but containers are not ready: waiting to be scheduled or pulling images
Running bound to a node; at least one container is running, starting or restarting
Succeeded all containers ended successfully and will not restart
Failed all containers ended and at least one ended in failure
Unknown the Pod's state could not be obtained, usually a problem reaching the node
  • restartPolicy is Always (the default), OnFailure or Never
  • Restarts back off: 10s, 20s, 40s and so on, capped at 300 seconds (5 minutes)
  • CrashLoopBackOff is a status you see in kubectl, not a Pod phase
Exam tip

There are five phases only; a repeated crash shows as CrashLoopBackOff in the status, not as a new phase.

Probes: Startup, Liveness and Readiness

  • Startup probe: has the app started? Until it succeeds, the other probes wait
  • Liveness probe: is the container still healthy? If it fails, the kubelet restarts the container
  • Readiness probe: can it take traffic? If it fails, the Pod is removed from Service endpoints, not restarted
  • Checks can be an HTTP request, a TCP connection, a command or gRPC; by default a probe runs every 10 seconds and fails after 3 failures

Probes on the storefront container

containers:
- name: storefront
  image: harborbooks/storefront:1.4
  readinessProbe:
    httpGet:
      path: /ready
      port: 8080
    periodSeconds: 10
  livenessProbe:
    tcpSocket:
      port: 8080
Exam tip

Liveness restarts the container; readiness only stops traffic.

4ReplicaSet, Deployment, rolling update, rollback

ReplicaSet and Deployment: Who Owns Whom

  • A ReplicaSet keeps a set number of identical Pods running; it finds them with a selector and creates new ones from a Pod template
  • It owns its Pods through ownerReferences
  • A Deployment creates and manages ReplicaSets: during a rollout there are two, the new one scaling up and the old one scaling down
  • The docs recommend a Deployment instead of a bare ReplicaSet

Exam tip

You normally create a Deployment; the ReplicaSet and the Pods follow from it.

The Deployment and the Rolling Update

  • A Deployment declares the desired state: how many Pods (replicas), which Pods (selector) and what each looks like (template)
  • A rollout starts only when the Pod template changes, for example a new image; changing replicas just scales
  • The default strategy is RollingUpdate: maxSurge and maxUnavailable are both 25%, so during an update at most 125% and at least 75% of the desired Pods exist
  • The other strategy is Recreate

A Deployment for the storefront

kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: storefront}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: storefront}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: storefront
        image: harborbooks/storefront:1.4
Exam tip

Change the Pod template to roll out; change replicas to scale.

Rollout History and Rollback

  • set image changes the Pod template, which starts a rollout
  • rollout status watches it, rollout history lists the revisions, and rollout undo returns to the previous revision or, with --to-revision, to a chosen one
  • A Deployment keeps 10 old ReplicaSets by default (revisionHistoryLimit) so that it can roll back
  • A rollout that cannot make progress is reported after 600 seconds by default (progressDeadlineSeconds)

Update the storefront, watch the rollout and roll back

kubectl set image deployment/storefront \
  storefront=harborbooks/storefront:1.5
kubectl rollout status deployment/storefront
kubectl rollout history deployment/storefront
kubectl rollout undo deployment/storefront
kubectl rollout undo deployment/storefront --to-revision=2
Exam tip

rollout undo is the rollback command; the old ReplicaSets are what make it possible.

5StatefulSet

StatefulSet: Stable Identity and Storage

  • Use a StatefulSet when each Pod needs a stable name, stable storage and an ordered start
  • Pods are named name-0, name-1, name-2 and keep their identity when replaced
  • A headless Service gives each Pod its own DNS name; volumeClaimTemplates give each Pod its own volume
  • Pods start and update in order (OrderedReady is the default), and the volumes are kept by default when Pods are deleted or scaled down

Exam tip

Databases and clustered apps that must remember who they are belong in a StatefulSet.

6DaemonSet

DaemonSet: One Pod per Node

  • A DaemonSet keeps one copy of a Pod on every node, or on a chosen group of nodes
  • When a node joins, a Pod is added; when a node leaves, its Pod is garbage collected; deleting the DaemonSet removes its Pods
  • Typical uses: a logs collection daemon, a node monitoring daemon, a cluster storage daemon
  • Harbor Books: a log collector on every node

Exam tip

"One on every node" means DaemonSet; it has no replica count.

7Job and CronJob

Job and CronJob: Work That Ends

  • A Job runs Pods until a set number finish successfully, and retries failures (backoffLimit defaults to 6)
  • A Job's Pods use restartPolicy OnFailure or Never; a Deployment allows only Always
  • A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule written in cron syntax: minute, hour, day of the month, month, day of the week
  • concurrencyPolicy is Allow (the default), Forbid or Replace

The nightly sales report as a CronJob

kind: CronJob
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
          - name: report
            image: harborbooks/report:1.2
Exam tip

Work that must finish is a Job; work that repeats on a schedule is a CronJob.

8Choosing the right controller

Choosing the Right Controller

  • Does the work end? Once: Job. On a schedule: CronJob
  • Does it run on every node? DaemonSet
  • Does each Pod need a stable name and its own volume? StatefulSet
  • Otherwise, for replaceable Pods: Deployment

Exam tip

Work out the nature of the workload first; the object follows.

What the Exam Asks: Workloads

  • Pod or container: the Pod is what is scheduled and managed
  • Liveness or readiness: liveness restarts; readiness stops traffic
  • Deployment or StatefulSet: replaceable Pods or named, sticky Pods
  • Scale or roll out: replicas scales; the Pod template rolls out
  • DaemonSet or replicas: a DaemonSet follows nodes, not a count
  • Job or CronJob: once or on a schedule
Exam tip

Name the need first, then the object that fits.

9Exam Q&A

9.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1Which statement describes a Pod?

  • AA group of worker nodes that report to the same control plane and API
  • BA packaged container image kept in a registry so that nodes can pull it
  • COne or more containers that run together and share network and storage
  • DA virtual machine that the scheduler places on a single worker node
Show the answer

Answer: C. A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes deploys: one or more containers that share an IP address and storage and are scheduled together. A group of nodes is a cluster, an image is the template a container starts from, and a Pod is not a virtual machine.

S2Harbor Books runs a Pod with an app container that serves the shop and a second container that ships its logs. How can the log shipper reach the app?

  • AOver localhost, because the containers share the Pod's IP address
  • BThrough a Service, because the containers of a Pod are isolated from each other
  • CThrough the node's disk, which the two containers use as a shared channel
  • DThrough a private IP address that the cluster gives to each container separately
Show the answer

Answer: A. Containers in one Pod share an IP address and port space, so they can reach each other on localhost. A Service is not needed inside a Pod, the Pod's volumes are not the only shared channel, and containers in a Pod do not get separate IP addresses.

S3A container's readiness probe fails, but its liveness probe still passes. What does Kubernetes do?

  • AIt restarts the container, because any failed probe means the container is broken
  • BIt deletes the Pod and asks the controller to create a new one on another node
  • CIt marks the Pod as Failed, because a probe did not succeed within its timeout
  • DIt keeps the container running and stops sending Service traffic to that Pod
Show the answer

Answer: D. A failed readiness probe removes the Pod from the Service's endpoints, so it gets no traffic, while the container keeps running. Only a failed liveness or startup probe leads to a restart, and a probe failure does not change the Pod phase to Failed.

S4The orders service needs about two minutes to start, and its liveness probe keeps killing it before it is ready. Which change fits best?

  • ARemove the readiness probe so that traffic reaches the Pod while it starts
  • BAdd a startup probe so that liveness checks wait until the app has started
  • CLower the liveness probe's period so that real failures are found sooner
  • DSet the Pod's restart policy to Never so that the container is not restarted
Show the answer

Answer: B. A startup probe holds back the liveness and readiness probes until the app has started, so a slow start is not mistaken for a failure. Removing readiness, checking more often or stopping restarts does not give the app time to start.

S5The storefront Deployment runs four replicas. The team changes the container image tag in its Pod template and applies the file. What happens?

  • AAll four Pods are deleted at once and four new Pods start from the new image
  • BA new ReplicaSet is created and Pods are replaced gradually by the new image
  • CNothing changes until someone runs a command to restart the existing Pods
  • DThe existing ReplicaSet is edited in place and its Pods restart one by one
Show the answer

Answer: B. Changing the Pod template triggers a rollout: the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and, under the default RollingUpdate strategy, scales it up while scaling the old one down. Deleting all Pods first is the Recreate strategy, which is not the default, and no manual restart is needed.

S6A new release is faulty. Which command returns the Deployment named storefront to its previous revision?

  • Akubectl scale deployment/storefront --replicas=0
  • Bkubectl rollout restart deployment/storefront
  • Ckubectl rollout pause deployment/storefront
  • Dkubectl rollout undo deployment/storefront
Show the answer

Answer: D. rollout undo returns to the previous revision, or to a chosen one with --to-revision. Scaling to zero stops the app, a restart re-creates Pods from the same faulty template, and pause only halts further rollout steps.

S7Harbor Books runs a database in which every replica needs its own persistent volume and a stable, predictable name. Which workload object fits?

  • AA StatefulSet, with a headless Service and volume claim templates
  • BA Deployment whose replicas share a single persistent volume
  • CA DaemonSet, so that a database Pod runs on each node in the cluster
  • DA Job, so that the database runs as a batch task until it is complete
Show the answer

Answer: A. A StatefulSet gives each Pod a stable name and its own volume through volume claim templates, with a headless Service for stable DNS names. A Deployment's replicas are interchangeable, a DaemonSet places one Pod per node, and a Job is for work that finishes.

S8Which statement about a DaemonSet is correct?

  • AIt keeps a fixed number of identical Pods running, wherever the scheduler puts them
  • BIt gives each of its Pods a stable name and its own persistent volume by default
  • CIt runs a copy of its Pod on each matching node and adds one when a node joins
  • DIt runs a Pod to completion and then stops creating Pods once the work is done
Show the answer

Answer: C. A DaemonSet follows nodes, not a replica count: one copy per matching node, and a new copy when a node joins. A fixed number of Pods describes a ReplicaSet or Deployment, stable names and volumes describe a StatefulSet, and running to completion describes a Job.

S9Harbor Books must build its sales report every night at two in the morning, and the work ends when the report is built. Which object fits?

  • AA Deployment with one replica that sleeps until the scheduled time arrives
  • BA Job, which repeats itself every night once it has been created
  • CA DaemonSet that wakes up on each node at the scheduled hour of the night
  • DA CronJob, which creates a new Job at the time its schedule says
Show the answer

Answer: D. A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule, and each Job runs to completion. A Job alone runs once, and a Deployment or a DaemonSet keeps its Pods running instead of letting them finish.

S10Which pairing of workload and object is a poor match?

  • AA stateless web front end that is replicated for availability: a Deployment
  • BA log collector that runs on each node of the cluster: a DaemonSet
  • CA database that needs stable names and its own volumes: a Deployment
  • DA one-off data migration that runs to completion: a Job
Show the answer

Answer: C. A database that needs stable names and its own volumes belongs in a StatefulSet, because a Deployment's Pods are interchangeable. The other three pairings are correct.

10Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Pod one or more containers with shared network and storage, scheduled together and replaced, not moved
Containers and probes init containers finish; sidecars keep running; liveness restarts, readiness stops traffic
Deployment manages ReplicaSets; a Pod template change rolls out; rollout undo goes back
StatefulSet and DaemonSet stable names and volumes, or one Pod per node
Job and CronJob work that ends, once or on a schedule
